confusionCorner.title: c Moves the Vertex, Not a
confusionCorner.body: The vertex of $ y = ax^2 + c $ is always $ (0, c) $, regardless of $ a $. Changing $ a $ stretches or shrinks the parabola and may flip it, but the vertex stays on the y-axis at $ y = c $.

formulaCard.title: Vertex of f(x) = ax² + c

explanation: The function $ f(x) = ax^2 + c $ is a vertical translation of $ f(x) = ax^2 $.
When $ c > 0 $, the graph shifts [[imp:up]] by $ c $ units. When $ c < 0 $, it shifts [[imp:down]] by $ |c| $ units.
The [[kw:vertex]] moves from $ (0, 0) $ to $ (0, c) $. The [[kw:axis of symmetry]] remains $ x = 0 $.
The shape (width and direction) is still determined by $ a $.
Example: $ g(x) = x^2 + 2 $ is the parent parabola shifted up 2 units. Vertex: $ (0,2) $.

Write g(x)=x²−2. Say: 'When c is negative, the whole parabola slides down. The axis of symmetry stays x=0.'

confusionCorner.body: Start with the parent $ y = x^2 $. First, apply the stretch/shrink and reflection from $ a $. Then shift the whole thing up or down by $ c $. The vertex goes from (0,0) to (0,c) after the shift.

formulaCard.title: General Form: f(x) = ax² + c
notes: Domain: all real numbers. Range: $ y \ge c $ if $ a > 0 $; $ y \le c $ if $ a < 0 $.

explanation: For $ f(x) = ax^2 + c $, the transformations from the parent $ y = x^2 $ are:
1) Vertical stretch or shrink by $ |a| $, with reflection if $ a < 0 $.
2) Vertical translation by $ c $ units.
The vertex is at $ (0, c) $, axis of symmetry $ x = 0 $.
Example: $ g(x) = 4x^2 + 1 $ is a vertical stretch by 4 (narrower) and a shift up 1 unit. Vertex $ (0,1) $.
Example: $ h(x) = -\frac{1}{4}x^2 + 4 $ is a vertical shrink by $ \frac{1}{4} $ (wider), a reflection in the x-axis, and a shift up 4 units. Vertex $ (0,4) $.

Write $ h(x) = -\frac{1}{4}x^2 + 4 $. Say: 'This opens down, is wider, and the vertex is at (0,4).'

discoveryHook.scenario: Now combine everything! The coefficient a stretches or shrinks the parabola, and c lifts or drops it. You can describe any $ y = ax^2 + c $ graph with just two numbers: a for shape and direction, c for the vertex's height.

blocks.title: Zeros of f(x) = ax² + c and Real-Life Problems

discoveryHook.scenario: When an egg is dropped from 64 feet, its height is modeled by $ f(t) = -16t^2 + 64 $. The moment it hits the ground is the zero of this function — the t-value when height equals 0. Finding zeros tells us when real-world events happen!

explanation: A [[kw:zero]] of a function $ f $ is an x-value for which $ f(x) = 0 $. It is also the x-intercept of the graph.
For $ f(x) = ax^2 + c $, set $ ax^2 + c = 0 $ and solve: $ x^2 = -c/a $.
Real zeros exist only if $ -c/a \ge 0 $ (i.e., $ c $ and $ a $ have opposite signs).
Real-life example: $ f(t) = -16t^2 + s_0 $ models height of a dropped object. The zero is when it hits the ground.
Example: $ -16t^2 + 64 = 0 $ → $ t^2 = 4 $ → $ t = 2 $ seconds (positive root only).

visuals.title: Blueprint Summary for f(x) = ax² + c

explanation: Understand: Identify $ a $ and $ c $. $ a $ controls direction (up if $ a>0 $, down if $ a<0 $) and width (stretch if $ |a|>1 $, shrink if $ 0<|a|<1 $). $ c $ sets the vertex $ (0,c) $.
Solve: To graph, note vertex $ (0,c) $, axis $ x=0 $. Plot symmetric points. To find zeros, solve $ ax^2 + c = 0 $.
Conclude: State domain (all reals), range ($ y \ge c $ if $ a>0 $; $ y \le c $ if $ a<0 $). Interpret zeros in context (time of impact, width at ground level, etc.).
Vertical translations $ g(x) = f(x) + k $ shift the vertex by $ k $ units and change the constant term.

confusionCorner.title: Zeros Move with c
confusionCorner.body: Increasing $ c $ (shifting up) moves zeros closer together, or eliminates them entirely if the vertex rises above the x-axis. Decreasing $ c $ (shifting down) spreads zeros farther apart.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Transformations & Zeros of f(x) = ax² + c

steps: Understand: $ a = -1/2 $, $ c = 8 $. Opens down (a<0). $|a|=1/2<1$ → wider shrink.
Solve: Vertex (0,8). Axis x=0. Zeros: $ -\frac{1}{2}x^2 + 8 = 0 $ → $ x^2 = 16 $ → $ x = \pm 4 $.
Conclude: Domain all reals, range $ y \le 8 $.
